name: Losar in the Darjeeling hills
when: February or early March, first day of the first Tibetan month (lunar)
summary: Losar is the Tibetan new year, kept by Tibetan, Sherpa, Bhutia and other Buddhist families across the hills. Monasteries in Ghum, Darjeeling, Mirik and Kalimpong hold prayers, homes are cleaned and decorated, and families share khapse biscuits, butter tea and visits for the first days of the year.
body: Losar marks the start of the Tibetan lunar year and usually falls in February or early March. In the Darjeeling hills it belongs to the Buddhist communities who have lived here for generations or came after 1959: Tibetan, Sherpa, Bhutia, Yolmo and others. Monasteries such as Yiga Choeling at Ghum, the Druk Sangag Choeling monastery at Dali on the Darjeeling road, Bokar Monastery above Mirik and Zang Dhok Palri Phodang in Kalimpong mark the days with long prayer sessions, butter lamps and new prayer flags.

The work starts before the new year. Houses are cleaned, old flags come down, and families fry khapse, the twisted biscuits made for the season. On the last days of the old year many monasteries hold rituals to clear away misfortune, and some stage masked cham dances. On Losar itself families visit the monastery early, then each other, sharing butter tea, chang and sweets. Prayer flags go up on ridges and rooftops around Ghum and Kalimpong.

Two other new year days fall close by. The Tamang community celebrates Sonam Lhochhar, usually in January or February, and the Gurung community keeps Tamu Lhosar at the end of December, with dances and gatherings in Darjeeling. For visitors Losar is mostly a community and family occasion rather than a staged show, so visit monasteries quietly and respectfully. Dates follow the lunar calendar; check current status before you travel.
tips: Visit Ghum Monastery early on the morning of Losar, when families come to offer prayers, and stay at the back of the hall.
Ask before photographing monks, rituals or families, and never use flash inside a prayer hall.
Walk clockwise around stupas and prayer wheels, and keep to the left of any shrine.

faqs.q: When is Losar celebrated in Darjeeling?
faqs.a: Losar falls on the first day of the first month of the Tibetan lunar calendar, usually in February or early March. Monasteries often hold rituals in the days before, and celebrations continue for about three days. The date changes every year, so check current status before you travel and confirm with the monastery you want to visit.

faqs.q: Where can tourists see Losar in the Darjeeling hills?
faqs.a: Ghum Monastery and the Dali monastery near Darjeeling, Bokar Monastery above Mirik and Zang Dhok Palri Phodang on Durpin Hill in Kalimpong are the easiest to visit. Expect prayers, butter lamps and new prayer flags rather than a fixed programme. Masked dances happen at some monasteries in the days before the new year, not every year.

faqs.q: Can non-Buddhists visit monasteries during Losar?
faqs.a: Yes, visitors are generally welcome in the courtyards and prayer halls. Dress modestly, remove shoes where asked, keep your voice low, walk clockwise and do not sit with your feet pointing at the altar. A small offering at the shrine is customary but never required. Some inner rooms may be closed to visitors.

faqs.q: Is February a good time to visit Darjeeling for Losar?
faqs.a: It is a quiet, cold month: Darjeeling is about 4 to 11 °C, hotels are cheap and mornings are often clear. Tea gardens are dormant, and snow is possible at Sandakphu and Lava. Pack thermals and a down jacket, since many budget rooms have no heating.

name: Dashain in Darjeeling
when: September–October, 15 days ending on the full moon of Ashwin (lunar)
summary: Dashain is the biggest festival of the Nepali-speaking Gorkha community, and in the Darjeeling hills it is the year's great homecoming. Barley shoots called jamara are grown for nine days, and on Vijaya Dashami elders place red tika and jamara on younger relatives with blessings.
body: Dashain runs for fifteen days in the lunar month of Ashwin, usually in late September or October, and honours the goddess Durga's victory over evil. For the Gorkha families who make up most of the hill population, it matters as much for family as for worship. Schools and offices close, people who work in Siliguri, Kolkata or further away come home, and the hills fill with visitors at the same time, since Durga Puja falls in the same days for Bengal.

The festival starts on Ghatasthapana, when a household sows barley or maize in a pot of sand and soil kept in a dark corner of the prayer room. The yellow shoots that grow over nine days are the jamara. On the tenth day, Vijaya Dashami, elders mix rice, yoghurt and red colour into tika, press it on the foreheads of younger family members, tuck jamara behind their ears and give blessings and a little money. Visits continue for days until the full moon.

Food is the other half of Dashain. Families make sel roti, the ring-shaped rice bread, along with meat curries, achar and sweets, and markets in Darjeeling and Kalimpong sell new clothes, marigolds and goats. For travellers it is a lively time but also a crowded one: shared jeeps fill fast and many local shops close on the main tika days. Dates follow the lunar calendar; check current status before you travel.
tips: Book rooms, trains and jeeps two to three months ahead; Dashain overlaps Durga Puja, the busiest week of the year in the hills.
Expect shops, cafes and drivers to take the main tika days off, and plan meals and transfers around them.
If a homestay family invites you to receive tika, accept with both hands joined and bow your head; it is a real blessing, not a show.

faqs.q: When is Dashain in 2026 and how long does it last?
faqs.a: Dashain lasts fifteen days in the lunar month of Ashwin, from Ghatasthapana to the full moon, usually in late September or October. The main tika day is Vijaya Dashami, the tenth day, which falls close to Durga Puja's Dashami in Bengal. Dates change every year, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What is jamara and tika at Dashain?
faqs.a: Jamara are barley or maize shoots grown in the dark for nine days from Ghatasthapana, which turn yellow. Tika is a paste of rice, yoghurt and red colour. On Vijaya Dashami elders place tika on the foreheads of younger relatives, tuck jamara behind their ears and give blessings and a small gift of money.

faqs.q: Is Darjeeling crowded during Dashain and Durga Puja?
faqs.a: Yes. Dashain overlaps Durga Puja, so visitors from Bengal arrive just as local families travel home. Hotels, trains and shared jeeps fill weeks ahead and prices rise. Book two to three months early, travel up in the morning, and keep plans flexible on the main tika days, when many businesses close.

faqs.q: Can tourists take part in Dashain?
faqs.a: Dashain is mainly celebrated at home, so the best way to see it is through a homestay family, who may invite you to receive tika. In towns you will see markets, marigolds and families visiting in new clothes. Respect the private nature of the day and ask before photographing people.

name: Tihar in Kalimpong
when: October–November, five days around the new moon of Kartik (lunar)
summary: Tihar is the five-day Gorkha festival of lights, held around Diwali. Each day honours someone: crows, dogs, cows, then oxen and the self, and finally brothers. In Kalimpong and the Darjeeling hills, homes glow with lamps and marigold garlands, and groups go house to house singing deusi and bhailo.
body: Tihar falls about three weeks after Dashain, around the new moon of Kartik, usually in late October or November, at the same time as Diwali. It lasts five days, and each one honours a different being. Kag Tihar offers food to crows, Kukur Tihar garlands dogs with marigolds and gives them a red tika and a good meal, and on the third day families worship the cow in the morning and Laxmi, goddess of wealth, in the evening with oil lamps and candles in every window.

The fourth day is kept in different ways: many families honour oxen, and some communities perform a puja for the self. On the fifth day, Bhai Tika, sisters give their brothers a seven-coloured tika, a garland of makhamali flowers, which hold their colour for weeks, and blessings for long life. Brothers give gifts in return. Through the evenings, groups of young people and children go from house to house singing bhailo and deusi songs, and are given money, fruit and sel roti.

Kalimpong is a good place to see Tihar. The town is smaller and less crowded than Darjeeling, homes along the ridge are lit with lamps and fairy lights, and deusi groups move through the neighbourhoods. Walk the town after dark on Laxmi Puja night and you will hear the songs from street to street. Dates follow the lunar calendar; check current status before you travel.
tips: Walk Kalimpong's neighbourhoods after dark on Laxmi Puja night to see the lamps; carry a torch for the steep lanes.
If a deusi group sings at your homestay, a small gift of money is the custom; your hosts will show you how much.
Expect fireworks on the main nights; keep pets and small children indoors and choose rooms away from the bazaar if you sleep lightly.

faqs.q: When is Tihar celebrated in Kalimpong?
faqs.a: Tihar lasts five days around the new moon of the lunar month of Kartik, usually in late October or November, alongside Diwali. Laxmi Puja falls on the third day and Bhai Tika on the fifth. The date moves every year, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What happens on each day of Tihar?
faqs.a: Day one, Kag Tihar, honours crows with food. Day two, Kukur Tihar, honours dogs with garlands, tika and treats. Day three is for the cow in the morning and Laxmi Puja with lamps at night. Day four honours oxen, or the self in some communities. Day five is Bhai Tika, when sisters bless their brothers.

They are the songs of Tihar. Groups go house to house in the evenings singing call-and-response verses, bhailo traditionally by girls and deusi by boys, though mixed groups are common now. The household gives money, fruit or sel roti, and the singers bless the home before moving on.

faqs.q: Is Tihar a good time to visit Kalimpong?
faqs.a: Yes. Late October and November are among the clearest months for mountain views, and the festival adds lamps, songs and garlands to the evenings. Rooms fill around the main days, especially when Tihar coincides with Diwali holidays, so book ahead. Some shops close on Laxmi Puja and Bhai Tika.
